summary: Defines an algorithm that finds, in an email message, the identity of the party that appears to have most directly caused the message to be delivered. This identity is the Purported Responsible Address. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives a rule for working out which party a message says was the last one to put it into the mail system, by looking only at the headers. The result is called the Purported Responsible Address, and the word purported is there because the headers can lie.

subtitle: A rule for finding, from the headers alone, who a message says last put it into the mail system.

tldr.problem: A message may be passed on by a forwarding agent, a mailing list server or a web site, so the person who wrote it is not always the party that introduced it into the mail system, and there was no agreed way to name that party.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a six-step algorithm that inspects the message headers, in order, for a Resent-Sender, a Resent-From, a Sender or a From header, and returns the single mailbox it finds as the Purported Responsible Address.
tldr.outcome: The address is only what the message claims about itself, and the RFC says so. It is an Experimental memo, the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 4407 is an April 2006 Experimental memo published alongside RFC 4405, RFC 4406 and RFC 4408 to document two approaches the MARID working group could not reconcile, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the Purported Responsible Address algorithm.

sections.title: Why a Message Needs a Responsible Party
sections.content:
Most e-mail flows relatively directly from a sender to a recipient, with a small number of mail transfer agents in between. Some messages are resent by forwarding agents, mailing list servers and other such software, and these messages effectively result in two or more mail transactions: one from the sender to the forwarding agent, and another from the agent to the destination. In some cases messages travel through more than one of these agents, which happens when one mailing list is subscribed to another, or when the address subscribed to a mailing list is a forwarding service.

The situation is further complicated because the party that introduces a message is often not the author of the message. Many news web sites have a function that lets the public e-mail a copy of an article to a friend. In that case the mail is from the person who pressed the button, but it is physically sent by the operator of the web site.

The RFC defines an identity associated with an e-mail message, the Purported Responsible Address, determined by inspecting the header of the message, and designed to be the entity that, according to the header, most recently caused the message to be delivered. The results of the algorithm are only as truthful as the headers in the message, so a message with fraudulent or incorrect headers yields an incorrect result. That is why the identity is called the purported responsible address: it tells what a message claims about where it came from, not necessarily where it actually came from.

The memo does not prescribe any particular use for the address. It notes that RFC 4406 describes a method of determining whether a particular mail transfer agent is authorized to send mail on behalf of the domain contained in the address.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message is forwarded or sent on by a list server, the party that put it into the mail system is not the person who wrote it. This RFC names that party, and works it out from the headers alone.

sections.title: Selecting the Header
sections.content:
The algorithm for determining the purported responsible address begins by looking at the resent headers, which a forwarding agent adds.

Step 1 selects the first non-empty Resent-Sender header in the message. If no such header is found, the algorithm continues with step 2. If it is found, the algorithm checks whether it is preceded by a non-empty Resent-From header and whether one or more Received or Return-Path headers occur after that Resent-From header and before the Resent-Sender header. If they do, the algorithm continues with step 2. Otherwise it proceeds to step 5.

Step 2 selects the first non-empty Resent-From header in the message. If a Resent-From header is found, the algorithm proceeds to step 5, and otherwise it continues with step 3.

Step 3 selects all the non-empty Sender headers in the message. If there are no such headers, the algorithm continues with step 4. If there is exactly one such header, it proceeds to step 5. If there is more than one, it proceeds to step 6.

Step 4 selects all the non-empty From headers in the message. If there is exactly one such header, the algorithm continues with step 5, and otherwise it proceeds to step 6.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm looks for four headers, in a fixed order: Resent-Sender, Resent-From, Sender, then From. It takes the first one it finds, as long as there is only one of it.

sections.title: Returning the Address, and the Notes on Odd Headers
sections.content:
Step 5 says that a previous step has selected a single header from the message. If that header is malformed, for example if it appears to contain multiple mailboxes, or the single mailbox is hopelessly malformed, or the single mailbox does not contain a domain name, the algorithm continues with step 6. Otherwise it returns that single mailbox as the purported responsible address. Step 6 says that the message is ill-formed and that it is impossible to determine a purported responsible address.

For the purposes of the algorithm, a header field is non-empty if and only if it contains any non-whitespace characters. Header fields that are otherwise relevant but contain only whitespace are ignored and treated as if they were not present. Steps 1 and 2 extract the Resent-Sender or Resent-From header from the first resent block, as defined in section 3.6.6 of the message format specification, if there is one, and steps 3 and 4 extract the Sender or From header if there are no resent blocks.

What counts as a hopelessly malformed header or mailbox in step 5 is a matter for local policy. Such local policy will never cause two implementations to return different purported responsible addresses, but it may cause one implementation to return an address where another does not, and this will happen only with messages whose headers are of questionable legality. The memo also says that the algorithm's treatment of messages that are not in strict conformance with the message format specification should not be taken as requiring or recommending that any system accept such messages when it otherwise would not have done so. However, if a liberal implementation accepts such messages and wants their purported responsible addresses, it must use this algorithm.

Where messages conform to RFC 822 rather than RFC 2822, the algorithm can give unexpected results. An RFC 822 message should not normally contain more than one set of resent headers, and their placement is not specified nor required to be contiguous, so it is possible that the Resent-From header is selected even though a Resent-Sender header is present. Such cases are expected to be rare or non-existent in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: If the header found holds one good address, that address is the answer. If the headers are a mess, the answer is that no address can be determined. The rules for what counts as a mess are left to each system, and they are the only place where two systems could disagree.

sections.title: What the Purported Responsible Address Does Not Prove
sections.content:
The purported responsible address is extracted from message headers that have historically not been verified, so anyone using it for any purpose must be aware that the headers from which it is derived might be fraudulent, malicious, malformed and incorrect. RFC 4406 describes one mechanism for validating it.

A message's purported responsible address will often be extracted from a header field that is not normally displayed by existing mail user agent software. If the address is used as part of a mechanism to authenticate the origin of the message, the memo says the message should not be displayed with an indication of its authenticity, positive or negative, without the header field from which the address came also being displayed.

The memo was published together with RFC 4405, RFC 4406 and RFC 4408 as Experimental documents, because there was no general technical consensus and efforts to reconcile the two approaches had failed. The IESG took no position on which approach is to be preferred, cautioned that there are serious open issues for each approach and concerns about using them in tandem, and considered that documenting the different approaches does less harm than not documenting them.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is a claim made by the message, not a fact about the sender. Anyone using it to make a security decision has to check it against something else first.
